clinicalPearls: TBCK encodes TBC1-domain-containing kinase, which regulates mTORC1 signalling and Rab-mediated intracellular trafficking; inheritance is autosomal recessive.
A recurrent founder nonsense variant is prevalent in individuals of Puerto Rican (Boricua) ancestry.
Presentation is with profound neonatal or infantile hypotonia, global developmental delay and often absent speech and independent walking.
Distinctive coarse facial features are characteristic, sometimes with macroglossia and an open-mouth, full-faced appearance.
The severe phenotype is progressive, with leukoencephalopathy, epilepsy, respiratory insufficiency and premature death.
Reduced mTORC1 signalling with disturbed autophagy is the proposed mechanism, and some features overlap with storage and neurodegenerative disorders.
Respiratory failure and recurrent infection are major sources of morbidity and mortality.
Additional features may include optic atrophy, central or sensory visual impairment and dysautonomia.
reference.pathophysiology: TBCK on chromosome 4q24 encodes TBCK (TBC1-domain-containing kinase), a multidomain protein comprising a pseudokinase domain, a TBC (Tre2-Bub2-Cdc16) Rab-GAP domain and a rhodanese-like domain that regulates mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signalling and Rab-GTPase-mediated endolysosomal and vesicular trafficking, thereby shaping cell growth, autophagy and actin organisation. Biallelic loss-of-function variants, including a recurrent nonsense founder allele in the Puerto Rican population, reduce TBCK protein and downregulate mTORC1 signalling, while impaired autophagy and endolysosomal handling generate storage-like neuronal pathology. The consequence is a syndromic infantile hypotonia with global developmental delay and characteristic facies that, in severely affected children, evolves into a progressive encephaloneuronopathy with leukoencephalopathy and neurodegeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital myopathies and congenital muscular dystrophies
Lysosomal storage disorders such as the mucopolysaccharidoses (given the coarse facies)
Other syndromic causes of infantile hypotonia with developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing or a hypotonia gene panel (biallelic TBCK); targeted founder-variant testing where ancestry fits
MRI brain (white-matter or leukoencephalopathy changes, atrophy)
Creatine kinase and neuromuscular assessment to evaluate the hypotonia (qualitative)
redFlags: Neurological or developmental regression suggesting the progressive form
Bulbar dysfunction with feeding difficulty and faltering growth
reference.prognosis: Highly variable; milder cases survive into adulthood with a largely static intellectual disability, whereas the severe progressive (encephaloneuronopathy) form leads to neurodegeneration, respiratory failure and death in childhood.
pitfalls: Mislabelling as a primary neuromuscular disorder (such as a congenital myopathy) and halting the workup
Overlooking the recurrent founder variant in individuals of Puerto Rican ancestry
Allowing coarse facies to prompt an exclusively lysosomal-storage workup
Underestimating respiratory risk in an apparently stable child
references: Neuromuscular and neurodevelopmental genetics review literature
management: Manage supportively, as no disease-modifying treatment exists, focusing on the hypotonia, developmental, feeding and respiratory needs
Provide developmental therapies including physiotherapy, occupational and speech and language therapy for the profound hypotonia and global delay
Ensure safe nutrition with feeding and swallow assessment and gastrostomy feeding when required
Deliver respiratory support with secretion clearance, prompt infection treatment and assisted ventilation as respiratory insufficiency develops
Treat epilepsy with anticonvulsants under EEG-guided review
Involve paediatric palliative care in the severe progressive encephaloneuronopathy form
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with founder-variant testing in individuals of Puerto Rican ancestry
Coordinate care through paediatric neurology and a multidisciplinary team
